analysis.one_liner: Ends the rule keeping illegally searched evidence out of federal criminal trials, replacing it with capped damages payouts.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it drew zero cosponsors, was sent to a Senate subcommittee on February 24, 1989, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have abolished the exclusionary rule in federal criminal cases — the rule that keeps evidence out of trial when police obtain it through an illegal search or seizure. In its place, it would let a person whose rights were violated sue the federal government for damages, but capped at $25,000 total, with limited recovery for anyone convicted of a crime, and discipline for officers left to the discretion of their own agency. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal prosecutors and law enforcement agencies gain the most: under the bill, evidence obtained through an unconstitutional search would always be admissible in federal criminal trials [S2] [S3]. Aggrieved individuals would gain a new money remedy against the United States, which does not currently exist in this form, but it is capped at $25,000 including punitive damages, and anyone convicted of an offense tied to the illegal search could recover only actual physical injury and property damage [S3].

how_it_helps.text: For prosecutors and law enforcement agencies, the central benefit is that evidence from an illegal search could no longer be suppressed: the bill adds a provision stating that admissible evidence 'shall not be excluded' for Fourth Amendment violations, removing the main courtroom consequence for unlawful searches.

For agencies, officer discipline stays in-house: an officer is subject to discipline only if the employing federal agency, at its discretion, finds after a hearing that the officer acted without a good-faith belief that the search was constitutional.

The bill also gives victims of illegal searches a damages claim against the United States itself, with possible attorney fees — a remedy that ordinary people do not currently have against the federal government in this form, though it is capped and narrowed for anyone convicted.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall mainly on people searched or seized illegally by federal officers, who would lose the exclusionary rule — the remedy that currently keeps unlawfully obtained evidence out of a prosecution — in exchange for a lawsuit capped at $25,000. Taxpayers would fund the resulting damage judgments.
analysis.who_pays_short: People searched illegally; taxpayers fund claims

drawbacks.text: The substitute remedy is weak. Damages are capped at $25,000 total including punitive damages, and a person convicted of any offense involving the seized evidence can recover only actual physical injury and property damage — so an innocent person wrongfully raided could at most recover $25,000, and someone later convicted could not recover for the invasion of privacy at all.

The bill makes this capped damages route the exclusive civil remedy for Fourth Amendment violations by federal officers, which would bar existing suits against officers themselves, while discipline remains discretionary with the officer's own agency and applies only when the officer lacked a good-faith belief the search was constitutional.

Removing suppression eliminates the primary incentive for police to follow the Fourth Amendment: today, officers and prosecutors have a reason to get warrants and search lawfully because breaking the rules can cost them the case; under this bill the evidence comes in regardless, and the consequence shifts to a capped payment from the Treasury.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs to ordinary people outweigh the benefits. The one genuine gain — a federal damages remedy for illegal searches — is hedged on every side: a $25,000 cap, no recovery for privacy invasion by anyone convicted, an exclusive-remedy bar on suing officers, and discipline that only the employing agency can impose and only for bad-faith searches. What would be lost is the exclusionary rule, the mechanism that currently gives law enforcement a reason to respect the Fourth Amendment. As drafted, the bill trades a working rights protection for a largely symbolic one.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee and its Constitution subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on February 8, 1989, to eliminate the exclusionary rule in federal criminal proceedings and replace it with a damages action against the United States capped at $25,000.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on February 24, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution — the last action ever taken on it.

No other senator signed on: the bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors, no subcommittee or committee action, no floor vote, and no House companion action recorded, and it expired on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, people subjected to federal searches kept the exclusionary rule, meaning unlawfully obtained evidence can still be thrown out at trial. Law enforcement and prosecutors gained nothing; the bill's sponsor advanced the issue without ever having to defend the capped-remedy substitute in a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people kept existing search protections

for.name: Sen. Orrin G. Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not attract a single cosponsor; it was his only recorded action on it.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the Congress, sending it to its Constitution subcommittee on February 24, 1989, and never holding a markup, hearing, or vote.

against.name: Civil liberties and criminal defense groups
against.role: Outside opponents of exclusionary rule repeal
against.what_they_did: Long opposed eliminating the exclusionary rule, arguing it is the main protection against unlawful police searches.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the support is unknown; the bill's only sponsor was a Republican and it drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would remove the courtroom penalty for unconstitutional searches: any evidence, once otherwise admissible, could be used, and discipline for officers would rest entirely with the officer's own agency and only in bad-faith cases. For ordinary people, this weakens the main deterrent against unlawful searches.
Prosecutors would never lose a case's evidence over a Fourth Amendment violation, strengthening their hand at trial. The public cost is fewer checks on how the underlying evidence was gathered.
Defense lawyers rely on suppression motions over illegal searches as a core tool, and the bill would take that tool away while making the capped government lawsuit the exclusive remedy.

The government would take on new liability for illegal searches, paying judgments up to $25,000 per claim plus possible attorney fees — a real but bounded cost. Agencies would gain corresponding control over officer discipline.
